chapter: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
title: Muskogee's Pastime Theater and whether Oklahoma was segregated
summary: After Bailey's show collapsed Spikes joined Johnny in Muskogee and took over the Pastime, a theater in a Black neighborhood.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: And, uh, you mentioned also that you played Colorado. You played Colorado? Was that around that period, or was that later?

Yeah, that was...uh...you see, my brother... after went back to this Bill Bailey's Troubadours, he got tired, and he left it, and I went on with it. I wanted to see Chicago and New York, you see. I'd never been there. So he got off in Kansas City, and I went on to Chicago with the company, and then we went over to Elkhart, and that was the last I seen of the manager. I got stranded. [Laughs] He ran off and left all of us, and then my brother got a job playing in Muskogee, Oklahoma at the theater, and he wanted a band, and so he sent for us who got stranded up there, and we went down there, and after four, five months, the...the manager there went home, and then my brother and I took over the theater and run it a little while.
That was the Pastime Theater in Muskogee. I saw in one article that Past Time was two words, and another time it one word. Do you remember?
I think it's all one word.
Because Oklahoma was pretty much segregated then, wasn't it?

No, I don't know 'bout segregated, but is...it ...well, I'd say it was in a Negro neighborhood. And its patronage was all Negro, you know. Because it was on East Second Street down in there, and that was half-breds, y'know, and everything.
Because I've heard that Tulsa was less segregated than other parts of Oklahoma, that there was more mixing of people from all kinds of backgrounds in Tulsa but I don't know that much.
